One requirement, four ways

Slide the Ra limit and compare the current symbol, the older symbol, the grade number and the triangle marks for the same value.

Read the callout; Interactive

Read the callout

Ten short questions on the symbols, the lay, the older notations and what the numbers respond to.

  1. The older ISO 1302 symbol with a circle in its V, and Ra 3.2. May this surface be machined to reach Ra 3.2 µm? No: material removal is prohibited. The circle in the V prohibits material removal. Material removal is prohibited: the surface must not be machined or otherwise have material removed to meet this requirement.
  2. A current symbol with an open V, no connecting material-removal crossbar or circle, a separate identifying dash above the short leg, and Ra 6.3. Does this callout forbid machining the surface? No, any process is permitted. The V has no connecting material-removal crossbar or circle: it is the basic symbol. The separate floating dash identifies ISO 21920; it does not require machining. Any manufacturing process is permitted. This does not forbid machining; it simply does not require it.
  3. A symbol with a bar closing its V, a short separate dash above the short leg, and Ra 0.8. Which standard's graphic is this? ISO 21920-1 (current). The short separate dash above the short leg, touching neither leg, marks an ISO 21920-1 symbol. The older ISO 1302 graphic has no dash.
  4. A block of surface whose marks run front to back. An arrow shows the right side view looking at its right side. The marks run front to back. Which lay symbol belongs on this surface in the right side view? =. The right side view looks along the arrow. Marks running front to back are parallel to that view's plane of projection, so the symbol is =. The same surface takes ⊥ in the front view: the symbol depends on the view, not on the screen or page.
  5. A block of surface whose marks run front to back. An arrow shows the front view looking at its front. The marks run front to back. Which lay symbol belongs on this surface in the front view? ⊥. The front view looks along the arrow. Marks running front to back are perpendicular to that view's plane of projection, so the symbol is ⊥. The same surface takes = in the right side view: the symbol depends on the view, not on the screen or page.
  6. The grade number N8. An older drawing gives grade N8. What does that stand for? Ra 3.2 µm. N8 stands for Ra 3.2 µm (126 µin). Each step of the grade number doubles or halves the Ra value, near enough.
  7. Three downward triangles. In the catalog comparison, which Ra values sit beside three triangles? 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 µm. Three triangles sit beside Ra 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 µm. The catalog calls this comparison approximate, not rigorous. Read it as a rough historical guide, not as acceptance limits.
  8. A current symbol with Rz 6.3. Which N grade means the same as this Rz 6.3 µm requirement? None: grades are Ra values. Grade numbers each stand for an Ra value; N9 is Ra 6.3 µm, not Rz 6.3 µm. Ra and Rz measure different things, and how they compare depends on the shape of the profile, as the same-Ra experiment in the lab shows.
  9. One deep scratch crosses this otherwise even trace. Which number has the largest proportional change? Rt. In the lab, a scratch three times the mark height takes Rt from 7.10 to 23.4 µm, Rz from 6.65 to 10.5 µm and Ra from 1.55 to 1.88 µm. Rt spans the highest peak to the deepest valley over the whole length. Rz averages five section heights, diluting localized extremes; filtering can spread a scratch across section boundaries. Ra averages every point.
  10. A block of surface with parallel marks running front to back, and a stylus trace running left to right across them. The trace on this surface crosses the marks. Traced along the marks instead, Ra would be: Much smaller. In the lab, Ra is 1.55 µm across the marks and 0.328 µm along them: the stylus misses the marks when it runs beside them. Tracing across the lay is the usual choice, but a direction the drawing specifies governs.
What this lab leaves out

What this lab leaves out

The lab is a teaching model of one straight trace. A real measurement and a real acceptance decision involve more:

  • The instrument. A real stylus has a tip radius, and instruments apply a short-wavelength filter and remove the part’s form before filtering. The lab’s stylus is sharp and its part is flat.
  • The filter and parameters. This lab follows the older ISO 4287 teaching convention of five sections for Rz, with a Gaussian mean line having 50% transmission at λc. Dense samples resolve the narrow marks; numerical integration on a coarser grid computes the smooth mean line. This is not a compliant instrument or a complete ISO 21920 inspection setup, and a drawing or standard can call for other settings.
  • The decision. The lab compares one trace with one limit. The drawing and its standard say how many traces are taken, where, and how the results are judged.
  • The process. No trace shows whether material was removed. The process requirement is checked against how the part was made.
  • Scratches and pits. Whether an isolated flaw counts against a texture requirement is for the drawing and its standard to say.
  • Symbols. The drawings are schematic. The lay symbols are those of ISO 1302:2002; the lab writes the same symbols in the ISO 21920-1 lay position. Check the current standard before relying on one there. Inch-drawing (ASME) practice is not covered here.

Supporting detail

Addendum

Additional evidence, standards context, and background referenced from the main text.

  1. Machining/Milling/Milling Operations

    Addendum 1. How the inspection decides, and what its numbers are

    The part is kept as a list of every cut: the space each tool swept through. The top of the metal at any point is the raw top lowered by every cut that reaches that point. The inspection measures walls, floors, holes and chamfers at sampled locations on that surface, with numbers rounded to a hundredth of a millimetre. A display grid plus probes derived from each cut and drawing boundary look for excess metal and gouges. Passing means the modeled checks pass; it does not certify every point of a real surface. Removed volume is an estimate from the 0.25 mm grid; very small cuts can change the analytic surface without a resolved grid volume. Walls and holes pass within ±0.10 mm, the bore within ±0.05 mm, and floors and faces within ±0.05 mm.

    Tapped holes are accepted when their drilled diameter falls inside the minor-diameter limits for a 6H internal thread: 4.917 to 5.153 mm for M6×1, and 6.647 to 6.912 mm for M8×1.25. These are finished minor-diameter limits, used here as a teaching proxy for pilot quality; they are not universal tap-drill recommendations or a complete 6H inspection.

    Sources: Gühring’s metric table, page 46, distinguishes nominal tap-drill sizes from finished minor limits. Haas’s M6×1 example specifies a 5 mm tap drill and a 2P–3P chamfer, illustrating why the model’s 4P is not universal. Vermont Gage explains the separate thread and cylindrical gauge checks.

    Back to reference 1

  2. Machining/Milling/G-code and Toolpaths

    Addendum 2. How the simulator reads and runs a program

    Each line is read in the order a control carries out the parts of a line: feed rate, spindle speed and tool first, then the tool change, the spindle, coolant, the modes, the move, and last the program end. So S2500 M3 G1 X20 F100 starts the spindle before it moves. Two codes from one group on a line, such as G0 G1, are an error.

    The interpreter first reads the whole program, and a second machine runs it at once to find its path, its time and the first place it would stop; that is the path drawn before you press Play. Pressing Play runs the program again on the block, move by move. The metal, the vise and the tools are those of the simulator in Milling Operations: every cut is kept as the space the tool swept, and a move that would break a tool rule or hit the vise stops where it would happen.

    An arc’s end point has to be on its circle to within 0.005 mm or 0.1 % of the radius, whichever is larger. A rapid, or a feed with the spindle stopped, stops a hair short of the first metal it would touch. The volume removed is an estimate from a 0.25 mm grid.

    Back to reference 2

  3. Machining/Milling/Climb and Conventional Milling

    Addendum 3. When a rough or hard exterior can change the choice

    Conventional milling can be useful in a qualified first pass on a rough surface because its gradual entry can reduce the impact on a brittle cutting edge. Tooling guidance also documents specialized exceptions such as machining through titanium alpha case before returning to climb milling. That is not a rule to choose conventional whenever stock has rust or scale: the layer’s hardness and abrasiveness, the work material, tool grade and geometry, engagement, fixturing and the approved process all matter. Use the tooling manufacturer’s data and the method approved for the machine.

    Seco Tools’ mechanical-load guidance discusses rough-surfaced material and gradual entry; Kennametal’s titanium guidance gives the material-specific alpha-case exception.

    Back to reference 3

  4. Machining/Milling/Climb and Conventional Milling

    Addendum 4. Why some machines climb mill without trouble

    A feed drive can be designed to reduce backlash, for example with a preloaded ball nut. The important question is whether the machine controls that movement, not simply whether it is called CNC. The chip is the same shape either way; what changes is whether the machine can hold the table against the pull of the cut.

    Sources: Sandvik Coromant: down milling versus up milling explains chip formation, rubbing and the backlash condition. Harvey Performance: climb versus conventional milling describes the lifting and downward force tendencies in peripheral horizontal milling. The arrows illustrate directions; they do not calculate force magnitudes.

    Back to reference 4

  5. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Backlash and Lost Motion

    Addendum 5. Where the definition comes from

    Modern Machine Shop's column Eliminate Backlash From Machining Centers (Mike Lynch, 2000) defines backlash as “any non-movement that occurs during axis reversals.” This page uses the CourseWiki definition on Screw Threads: clearance that must be taken up after reversing before the load moves. In a real drive, elastic deflection can add lost motion as well; the lab below leaves it out.

    Back to reference 5

  6. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Backlash and Lost Motion

    Addendum 6. A readout that measures the slide, and when the clearance still matters

    The MIT 2.670 milling machine notes (section “Using the Micrometer Dials”) also point out that a digital readout measures the bed position directly, so its reading is not thrown off by backlash. The clearance is still in the drive. A force that pushes the carriage along the screw can move it across the clearance without the handwheel turning; Climb and Conventional Milling explains when a cutting force does that.

    Back to reference 6

  7. Machining/Milling/Feeds and Speeds

    Addendum 7. Feed per tooth is not always the thickness of the chip

    Feed per tooth is how far the work moves between teeth. The chip a tooth actually cuts is only that thick when the cutter is at least half buried across its diameter. In a narrower cut, each tooth meets the work at a slant and the chip comes out thinner. Climb and Conventional Milling shows this: at a width of cut of 10% of the diameter, the thickest part of the chip is 60% of the feed per tooth.

    Some cutting data raises the feed per tooth for narrow cuts to make up for this. Read what your data assumes before using its numbers, and ask if it does not say. Thinner chips also take more energy per cubic inch, which is one reason a power estimate is a band.

    The spindle-speed, table-feed and feed-per-tooth relations follow Sandvik Coromant’s milling formulas and definitions. The calculator’s cutting-speed and feed-per-tooth ranges are from GARR TOOL’s general purpose milling guide, and its cutting-energy bands are converted from Kennametal’s milling power factors.

    Sandvik’s specific cutting-force explanation shows why chip thickness and cutting-edge geometry affect the energy estimate. Haas’s spindle power curves illustrate why available power depends on RPM; read the machine’s own curve and duty rating rather than treating its headline horsepower as available everywhere.

    Back to reference 7

  8. Machining/Milling/Tool Stickout and Deflection

    Addendum 8. The calculation and its units

    The solid round section has area moment of inertia I = πd⁴/64. With x measured from the clamp, displacement magnitude is y(x) = Fx²(3L − x)/(6EI). At the tip, x = L, so δ = FL³/(3EI). Both displacement and slope are zero at x = 0.

    Use N for force, mm for length and diameter, and N/mm² for E. The controls show E in GPa: multiply by 1,000 to get N/mm². The answer is in mm; multiply by 1,000 for µm.

    For F = 100 N, L = 40 mm, d = 10 mm and E = 600 GPa, I = 490.874 mm⁴ and δ = 0.007243 mm = 7.243 µm. Halfway along that tool, y(L/2) is 5/16 of the tip value, or 2.264 µm. These are calculated examples, not measured cutter data.

    Back to reference 8

  9. Machining/Milling/Tool Stickout and Deflection

    Addendum 9. Primary references

    • MIT OpenCourseWare: review of cantilever beam theory, lecture 2 appendix, equations 10–11 on PDF page 5. Derives the end-loaded shape and tip displacement with fixed-clamp boundary conditions.
    • Hyperion Materials & Technologies: Carbide vs. Steel. Its wear-grade comparison reports the modulus range; it does not specify the stiffness of a particular fluted cutter.

    Back to reference 9

  10. Machining/Turning/Lathe Operations

    Addendum 10. Reference examples for these mechanisms

    Sherline’s lathe instructions show three-jaw and four-jaw chucks, a faceplate and the ordinary between-centers arrangement. Sherline’s collet description shows one representative split-collet and taper arrangement. Its drive-dog instructions distinguish the dog and drive plate from direct faceplate clamping.

    The steady-rest instructions show a rest fixed to the bed, while the follower-rest instructions show the rest attached to the saddle so it travels with the cutter. The drawings here explain those generic roles; they are not setup instructions or copies of manufacturer artwork.

    Back to reference 10

  11. Machining/Turning/Lathe Operations

    Addendum 11. Rake and chipbreakers depend on the whole cutting setup

    Rake describes the slope of the surface the chip flows over. Clearance keeps the tool below the edge from rubbing. Material matters, but hardness alone does not dictate positive, neutral or negative rake: tool material, edge strength, holder geometry and rigidity also matter. Use the tool maker's cutting geometry and range for the application.

    A chipbreaker guides a chip into a tighter curl so it can break. It may be molded into an insert or ground into a tool. It works within a range of feeds and depths; a very thin chip can curl without breaking. A chipbreaker is not a guarantee of short chips at every setting.

    Back to reference 11

  12. Machining/Turning/Lathe Operations

    Addendum 12. How a manual lathe keeps every pass on one helix

    The carriage is coupled to the leadscrew by closing the half-nut. On a lathe with an inch leadscrew cutting an inch thread, the thread dial shows when to close it so that each pass drops into the same groove. Many machinists also feed the tool in with the compound travel set near 30° from the radial cross-feed direction, so that most of the cut is taken by one flank of the tool.

    The simulator simplifies all of this. It keeps every pass on one helix for you, feeds the tool straight in, and checks a simplified 60° thread by its crest and root diameters. A real thread is checked against a thread table with thread gauges or measuring wires.

    Back to reference 12

  13. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

    Addendum 13. Why tooth counts work, and what the dashed circles mean

    The gears here share one tooth size, called module, and a 20° pressure angle. Their pitch diameters are proportional to tooth count. The dashed pitch circles roll together at equal tangential speed, so nA × NA = −nB × NB when clockwise is positive on both shafts. Here n is signed rotational speed and N is tooth count.

    Tooth flanks are involute curves. Actual tooth surfaces can slide during contact even though the pitch circles roll. The drawing samples those curves, simplifies the tooth roots and adds a small visual clearance. It is a motion model, not a manufacturing drawing.

    Back to reference 13

  14. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

    Addendum 14. Primary references and model boundaries

    • KHK: Idler gear. The intermediate tooth count cancels from the overall speed ratio.
    • KHK: Calculation of Gear Dimensions, section 4.1 and Table 4.1. Standard spur-gear pitch, base, tip and root dimensions and center spacing.
    • MIT OpenCourseWare: Gear Trains. Gear bodies, shared shafts, and force and torque balance.

    The lab assumes rigid external spur gears, fixed shaft centers, matched tooth size and steady transmitted load. It starts lossless; its efficiency control applies the same specified loss to every actual mesh, including both meshes around an idler. Acceleration, elasticity, backlash dynamics, detailed friction, noise and tooth strength are omitted. Changing tooth counts moves the centers to maintain the correct mesh; it does not represent swapping a gear into a fixed gearbox housing.

    Back to reference 14

  15. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

    Addendum 15. Why adding losses is only an approximation

    For a 1000 W input and three 96% stages, the losses are 40 W, 38.4 W and 36.864 W. Each 4% applies to a smaller incoming power. Adding 4% + 4% + 4% incorrectly takes every loss from the original 1000 W.

    Back to reference 15

  16. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

    Addendum 16. Follow both stages of one loaded train

    A 24-tooth driver at 1440 rpm and 4 lbf·ft drives 48 teeth. That shaft also carries a 15-tooth driver for a 45-tooth output. Both stages are 96% efficient, with no other losses. After stage 1: 720 rpm and 4 × 2 × 0.96 = 7.68 lbf·ft. The shared shaft carries that same 720 rpm into stage 2. Final output: 1440/(2 × 3) = 240 rpm and 7.68 × 3 × 0.96 = 22.1184 lbf·ft, versus 24 lbf·ft ideally. Overall efficiency is 0.9216.

    Back to reference 16

  17. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

    Addendum 17. Worked design: a winch with a speed ceiling and torque floor

    A motor supplies 1680 rpm and 24 lbf·ft. The output must be at most 40 rpm and at least 950 lbf·ft. Available gears have 10–60 teeth, with unlimited copies; each reduction stage is at most 6:1 and 97% efficient. There are no idlers or other losses.

    1. Speed requires i ≥ 1680/40 = 42. Two stages give at most 6² = 36, so try three.
    2. Three stages give ηtotal = 0.97³ = 0.912673. Torque requires i ≥ 950/(24 × 0.912673) ≈ 43.3708. Torque controls.
    3. Choose 12 → 48, 15 → 45, and 16 → 60 teeth: i = 4 × 3 × 3.75 = 45. Every tooth count and stage ratio meets its limit.
    4. ωout = 1680/45 ≈ 37.33 rpm ≤ 40 rpm. τout = 24 × 45 × 0.912673 = 985.68684 lbf·ft ≥ 950 lbf·ft. Both pass. Three external meshes make the output opposite to the input.

    This is one feasible train, not a claim of an optimum or a complete winch specification. For load force at a drum, continue to Torque; for travel speed, use Rotation and Linear Speed.

    Back to reference 17
